newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's souvenir industry cashes in on Pope.
newsitem.headline: France's souvenir industry cashes in on Pope.

text.p: Through the dark clouds looming over the French economy, a small ray of celestial light has broken: the souvenir industry is cashing in on Pope John Paul's visit this week.
From the sacred to the profane, souvenir merchants are offering papal candles, T-shirts, watches, medallions, keyrings, crockery and even champagne.
But there is a marked effort to keep things tasteful.

"The mayor asked us not to make too much of the commercial aspect of the visit," a shopkeeper in Tours, the Pope's first port of call on Thursday, told the daily France-Soir. "There's nothing tasteless, but that may be due less to virtue than to the parlous state of the local economy."
After a mediocre tourist season, there is not a hotel room spare in Tours, in western France, or Reims, northeast of Paris, where some 150,000 pilgrims are expected on Sunday.
And photographers are reported to have paid up to 10,000 francs ($2,000) for a balcony with a view over the papal route.

The high-point of the Pontiff's fifth pastoral visit to France will be at Reims, in the champagne-growing region, where he will celebrate the 1,500th anniversary of the baptism of Clovis, the first European monarch to convert to Catholicism.

In souvenir shops and wineries around the Gothic cathedral, three brands of Clovis champagne are on sale next to a wine named the "pope's flask" from Chateauneuf-du-Pape, near the former papal residence of Avignon.

There is Clovis mustard and vinegar, a bronze medallion of the baptism of the pagan fifth century warlord said to have been authorised by the archdiocese, and even a designer Clovis silk scarf for a hefty 850 francs ($170).

Commercial souvenir stalls will be banned at and around the air bases where the Pontiff will say mass in Tours and Reims, although church associations and youth groups will be selling their own papal accessories, including hats, bags and T-shirts.
